cards.title: Consolidate Performance Max for high signal density
cards.summary: Concentrate cold-traffic spend into one PMax campaign so Google gets dense conversion signals rather than fragmented ones.
cards.use_when: Setting up or restructuring Google Ads account structure for a store's cold acquisition, deciding whether to split one PMax campaign into many.
steps: Put the core cold acquisition budget into a single PMax campaign rather than spreading it across multiple campaigns and channels; the source argues this keeps signal density high so Google learns how to convert on the channel.
Use asset group exclusions and brand/non-brand segmentation within that structure instead of separate campaigns per channel.
Feed clean data: verify conversion tracking fires correctly on the purchase event and on any qualifying lead events you actually want optimized.
Push hardest on the product feed — product titles, images, descriptions — because the source calls feed optimization '90% of the game' for PMax performance.

If you have access to a Google rep (typically tied to spend level), use them for account support, and use a third-party PMax insight tool (the source names Microscript; verify current availability) to inspect asset-group and search-term level performance.
Exclude brand terms from cold campaigns so cold and returning demand can be judged separately.
caveats: PMax transparency has improved but is still not fully granular; results depend on spend level and feed quality.
The source's claim that a single consolidated campaign is always better reflects their own experience, not a universal rule — test against a segmented structure if you have data.

cards.title: Rebuild the PDP as a direct-response cold-traffic page
cards.summary: Convert an educational or bare product page into a structured persuasion flow that can sell unfamiliar cold visitors, not just loyal repeat buyers.
cards.use_when: A store is scaling into new audiences and its current PDP converts returning customers but stalls cold traffic.
steps: Audit the current PDP: if it is just product images plus a couple of FAQs, treat it as an educational page optimized for people who already know you.
Restructure the page into a persuasive flow that segments the cold visitor: what the product is, why it is different, why it is credible, why buy now.
Add explicit education for the unfamiliar visitor — if they need to understand the category (e.g. 'what is this ingredient'), the page must teach before it sells.
Insert objection handling answering the top reasons a cold visitor would hesitate to buy from you instead of a competitor.
Layer in trust builders and proof: founder story, third-party test results, reviews, relevant certifications.
Add comparison content against competitor alternatives so a shopper who is researching has the comparison done for them.
Close with a subscriber-first offer to capture the next purchase, not just this one.
Judge the change on cold-traffic conversion rate specifically, not blended site conversion.
caveats: The source reports conversion rate on cold traffic roughly doubling overnight for one methylene blue brand — a case result, not a benchmark.
Loyal customers convert on almost any page, so blended conversion rate masks whether the rewrite worked for cold traffic.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Build the full cold-traffic conversion mechanism, not just ads
cards.summary: Treat the ads, pre-sale page, PDP, order flow and after-sell as one system, because the page that receives the click determines whether the ad spend converts.
cards.use_when: Planning a cold acquisition push and deciding which assets must be built or fixed before raising spend.
steps: Define the chain end to end: YouTube/Google creative → pre-sale page → product page → checkout/order → post-purchase upsell/after-sell.
Write the ad creative and the landing page together so the promise made in the ad is answered immediately on the page.
Use the pre-sale page to educate and sell the idea of the brand before the PDP, particularly when the market is unsophisticated about the product.
Put an after-sell or upsell step after order to lift AOV and pull blended CAC down.
Assess how sophisticated the market is before writing anything: a market that already understands the product needs differentiation, not basic education; a market that doesn't needs education first.
Keep the whole system in-house or tightly coordinated, since disjointed vendors obscure which step is leaking.
caveats: The source is an agency describing its own full-funnel build; the same structure is achievable with in-house or mixed teams if the steps are owned by one accountable plan.
Pre-sale pages must comply with the ad platform's landing-page policies for regulated categories.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Design an objection-handling block sequence on the PDP
cards.summary: Build a PDP section order that moves a cold visitor from 'what is this' through objections, proof, comparison, then offer.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a PDP for a supplement, wellness or other considered-purchase product where cold visitors need convincing.
steps: Open with a clear statement of what the product is and the outcome it delivers, in plain language for someone who has never heard of the brand.
Follow with objection handling: price, skepticism about efficacy, safety concerns, subscription/commitment fears, 'why not the cheaper competitor'.
Add proof elements next — test results, third-party validation, review volume — placed where the skeptic is most likely to be reading.
Add a comparison section positioning the product against named or implied alternatives, since competitors will enter the market once a category gets attention.
Add FAQs that answer the questions support actually receives, not generic filler.
End with a strong subscriber-first offer (subscribe and save, first-order bundle) to capture repeat revenue from the first purchase.
Keep founder/credibility content visible — the source credits a strong founder image as part of why the brand held up against new entrants.
caveats: Requires real proof assets; inventing test results or reviews is both non-compliant and destructive.
Order matters less than completeness for some audiences — test section order rather than assuming one fixed sequence.

cards.title: Monitor the ad account daily to catch demand spikes
cards.summary: Check spend and impression behavior every day so search demand spikes from external events can be funded within hours, not missed.
cards.use_when: Running Google Ads for a category that can be featured in podcasts, news or social media and may spike suddenly.
steps: Log into the ad account daily, not weekly; the source's example spike was visible only to someone checking that morning.
Watch for the platform spending above the usual daily budget, which can signal rising available traffic (Google may overspend within the 30-day average).
Check external sources when spend jumps: the source traced a spike to a podcast episode that had run two hours earlier.
If the spike is genuine demand for your product, raise the budget aggressively rather than incrementally — in the source's case from roughly $2K to $20K per day for the spike window.
Track search impression share during the spike to see how much of the demand you are capturing (they reported roughly 70% at peak).
Hold the higher budget after the spike if performance supports it, rather than reverting automatically.
caveats: Aggressive budget raises assume your break-even CPA and conversion mechanism can absorb the volume without breaking profitability.
Competitor non-response is not guaranteed; in a well-funded category rivals may also raise budgets.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Run 30/60/90/180/365-day contribution math before deciding how much to pay per customer
cards.summary: Decide how aggressively to buy customers using long-window contribution data, not front-end profit on the first order.
cards.use_when: Setting target CPA, deciding whether to accept near break-even or loss-making first orders to win market share in a repeat-purchase category.
steps: Calculate contribution margin per order: price minus COGS minus shipping minus payment fees minus any variable fulfillment cost.
Build cohort windows at 30, 60, 90, 180 and 365 days and compute cumulative contribution per customer across each window, including repeat purchases, subscription revenue and upsells.
Define break-even CPA as the point where cumulative contribution equals acquisition cost over your chosen window.
If acquisition cost stays at or below break-even across the window, you can scale spend aggressively; if it exceeds it, the customer is not worth enough yet.
Treat the customer's worth as something you can increase: raise AOV, add upsells, improve repurchase and subscription rates rather than only cutting acquisition cost.
Recheck the model after any pricing, COGS or AOV change before using it to justify a bigger budget.
caveats: Long-window models assume retention and repurchase rates hold; new competitors or product changes can break that assumption.
The source's 'never went below break even' outcome is a case result for one brand, not a guarantee for your category.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Position 'RoRoaWAS' correctly: low is the goal
cards.summary: Understand that in this source's framing, a lower return-on-ad-spend-in-relation-to-a-window metric means faster payback, so low values are desirable.
cards.use_when: Reviewing ad reporting and reacting to a metric that looks counterintuitively weak or strong.
steps: Clarify which metric your account and tools are actually showing before acting on it — the source uses a ratio framed around payback window rather than the more common 'higher is better' ROAS.
Under this framing, a low value means you are getting your money back quickly; the source explicitly says you want low values.
Do not cut a campaign just because this metric looks low; check whether it reflects fast payback instead.
Pair the metric with the long-window contribution math so you know the true ceiling on what you can pay per customer.
Confirm the definition in your own reporting stack — terms like RoRoaWAS are not standardized and depend on how the window is defined.
caveats: This is the source's own metric framing, borrowed from ecommerce ad reporting conventions; definitions vary, so verify what your tool means by it before applying the rule.
A metric alone should not override contribution-margin math.

cards.title: Use YouTube as the scaling lever once search and shopping plateau
cards.summary: Add YouTube to the cold-traffic mix when search and shopping demand is fully captured, because it adds new top-of-funnel inventory.
cards.use_when: Google search, shopping and display spend has hit a ceiling and the store needs new cold audience volume.
steps: Confirm search and shopping are tapped out — the source reported roughly $2–4K/day max on high-search-volume days before adding YouTube.
Build a YouTube campaign structure that feeds the same conversion mechanism (pre-sale page and PDP) already proven on search.
Start with a small set of compliant creatives, then let spend concentrate on whichever one clears policy and performs; the source describes a single creative carrying $300–500/day early.
Expect YouTube to tolerate more frequency than search because inventory is far larger, easing creative fatigue relative to other channels.
Track new-customer acquisition separately from retargeting so you can attribute YouTube's incremental contribution.
Set the scaling target in new customers per month rather than only in spend.
caveats: The source's figures ($6.5K/day target, 10K+ new customers/month aim) are their own goals for one brand, not benchmarks.
A second brand mentioned had a break-even around 1.2–1.3 by their framing; break-even levels are store-specific.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Plan for creative volume to beat ad platform compliance filters
cards.summary: For regulated categories, build a creative production pipeline that produces enough compliant variants to find the few that both pass policy and convert.
cards.use_when: Running health, wellness or supplement ads on Google where policy review rejects most creative angles that work on Meta.
steps: Assume most creative that works on Meta will not clear Google policy in regulated categories — the source reports only one of a batch of Meta ads ran on Google.
Write and produce compliant first: remove prohibited claims, avoid medical claims, and keep language within the platform's health-category rules before you test.
Produce volume, not one polished ad; the goal is enough variants to survive review filtering and still leave a testable set.
Once creative clears policy, test aggressively for conversion and scale potential, concentrating spend on winners.
When creative is the bottleneck, add production capacity rather than cutting spend — the source says their bottleneck shifted from backend to creative once search, shopping and display were solved.
Re-verify current platform policy rules before each production cycle, since health ad policies change.
caveats: Compliance constraints are category and platform specific; some products (the source names methylene blue) are not allowable on most platforms at all.
Do not infer that compliant creative is less effective — the source's goal is to clear policy and still convert.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Set the LTV engine: front-end acquisition campaigns feeding email/SMS and upsells
cards.summary: Structure paid campaigns and retention flows as one engine where acquisition buys first orders and email, SMS and upsells produce the repeat value.
cards.use_when: Designing the relationship between acquisition campaigns and retention channels to justify higher cold-traffic spend.
steps: Separate the roles: search, shopping and display campaigns deliver first-touch points; email, SMS and post-purchase upsell flows produce repeat revenue.
Make sure every acquired customer is retargetable — capture email/SMS consent at purchase or via a subscriber-first offer.
Build post-purchase upsell and cross-sell flows so the first order is not the only revenue event.
Use the retention revenue in your contribution math to set how much you can pay for a first order.
Treat the quality of the backend as the scaling moat: if the customer is not worth enough, improve AOV, repeat purchase and subscription rather than only squeezing CPA.
Consult or plan product drops so there is something new to sell existing customers when acquisition volume rises.
caveats: High acquisition volume stresses fulfillment — the source flags that fulfillment will break if you push too many purchases before operations are ready.
Retention economics depend on a genuinely repeat-consumable product; one-time-purchase categories cannot support this model the same way.
cards.source_name: Ecommerce Google Ads Free Course (4+ Hours) _ Google & Shopify.docx

cards.title: Differentiate a PDP when competitors enter a validated category
cards.summary: When a category gets public attention and competitors flood in, replace first-mover advantage with evidence, clarity and differentiation on the page.
cards.use_when: A store's product category is being talked about publicly and new competitors are launching similar products.
steps: Anticipate new entrants as soon as your product starts working — the source predicted competitors entering their category well before they did.
Audit competitor product pages: the source found competitor pages had no education, no founder story, no differentiation and no brand feel.
Rework the funnel so evidence, clarity and differentiation appear at every step: ad, pre-sale page, PDP and post-purchase.
Dimensionalize the brand — tell the founder story and make the brand feel like a brand, not a white-label listing.
Maintain the positioning rather than relying on being first; first-mover status degrades once the category becomes known.
Keep the conversion mechanism strong enough that attention spikes convert to first orders you own, not to the category generally.
caveats: Some competitor pages may still convert on price alone; differentiation must be paired with a competitive offer.
The source's specific category example (methylene blue and public figures discussing it) is illustrative, not applicable to every product.
